These examples cover models beyond the basic univariate and bivariate workflow.
Read [Get started](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/example.html) first.
Each model section defines its own specification and simulated data.

- [Parameter settings](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/fitting-and-inference.html#parameter-settings) and [observed data and initial state](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/fitting-and-inference.html#observed-data-and-initial-state): Fitting and inference.
- [Calculation engines](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/computation.html#calculation-engines): Computation.
- [Residual diagnostics](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/fitting-and-inference.html#residual-process): Fitting and inference.

```{r}
library(emhawkes)
```

## More complex models

### Multi-kernel model

A multi-kernel Hawkes model requires `type_col_map` in its `hspec` object.
This list maps each event type to the corresponding columns of the kernel parameter matrices.
Consider a bivariate multi-kernel model:

$$
\lambda_t = \mu + \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(t-u) d N(u)
$$

where

$$
h = \sum_{k=1}^{K} h_k, \quad
h_k (t) = \alpha_k \circ \begin{bmatrix}
e^{-\beta_{k11} t} & e^{-\beta_{k12} t} \\
e^{-\beta_{k21} t} & e^{-\beta_{k22} t}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $k$ indexes the kernels, $\alpha_k$ is the excitation matrix for kernel $k$, and $\circ$ denotes elementwise multiplication.

For a bivariate Hawkes model with two kernels, the intensity processes are

$$
 \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(t) \\ \lambda_2(t) \end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{bmatrix} + \int_{-\infty}^{t} \begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_{111} e^{-\beta_{111}(t-s)} & \alpha_{112} e^{-\beta_{112}(t-s)} \\
\alpha_{121}e^{-\beta_{121}(t-s)} & \alpha_{122}e^{-\beta_{122}(t-s)}
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d N_1(s) \\ dN_2(s) \end{bmatrix} 
+ \int_{-\infty}^{t} \begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_{211} e^{-\beta_{211}(t-s)} & \alpha_{212} e^{-\beta_{212}(t-s)} \\
\alpha_{221}e^{-\beta_{221}(t-s)} & \alpha_{222}e^{-\beta_{222}(t-s)}
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d N_1(s) \\ dN_2(s) \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The parameter matrices are

$$
 \alpha = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{111} & \alpha_{112} & \alpha_{211} & \alpha_{212} \\ \alpha_{121} & \alpha_{122} & \alpha_{221} & \alpha_{222}
\end{bmatrix}, \quad
 \beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_{111} & \beta_{112} & \beta_{211} & \beta_{212} \\ \beta_{121} & \beta_{122} & \beta_{221} & \beta_{222}
\end{bmatrix} \quad
$$

The mapping must specify which columns correspond to each counting process $N_i$.

```{r}
mu <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.02), nrow=2)
      
beta_1 <- matrix(rep(10, 4), nrow=2) 
beta_2 <- matrix(rep(1, 4), nrow=2)
beta  <- cbind(beta_1, beta_2)
      
alpha_1 <- matrix(c(3, 2,
                    2, 3), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
alpha_2 <- matrix(c(0.3, 0.2,
                    0.2, 0.3), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
alpha <- cbind(alpha_1, alpha_2)

print(alpha)
```

The first and third columns of $\alpha$ correspond to $N_1$, and the second and fourth columns correspond to $N_2$.
Thus, define `type_col_map` as follows:

```{r}
type_col_map <- list(c(1,3),  # columns for dN1
                     c(2,4))  # columns for dN2
type_col_map
```

The entry `type_col_map[[i]]` lists the columns associated with event type `i`.
Rows of the intensity matrix identify event types.
After a type `i` event, `type_col_map[[i]]` selects the kernel columns to update.
Use this mapping to extract the corresponding parameters:

```{r}
cat("Part of alpha associated with N1: \n")
alpha[, type_col_map[[1]]]  # associated with N1
cat("Part of alpha associated with N2: \n")
alpha[, type_col_map[[2]]]  # associated with N2

cat("Part of beta associated with N1: \n")
beta[, type_col_map[[1]]]  # associated with N1
cat("Part of beta associated with N2: \n")
beta[, type_col_map[[2]]]  # associated with N2
```

```{r}
h <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta=beta, type_col_map = type_col_map)
h
```

For this multi-kernel model, `lambda_component0` must be supplied for both simulation and estimation.

```{r}
set.seed(620)
lambda_component0_mk <- matrix(seq(1, 1.7, 0.1), nrow = 2)
res_mk <- hsim(h, size = 3000, lambda_component0 = lambda_component0_mk)
res_mk
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit_mk <- hfit(h, res_mk$inter_arrival, res_mk$type,
               lambda_component0 = lambda_component0_mk,
               final_hessian = "stable")
summary(fit_mk)
```

This example explicitly requests the checked final Hessian. The original estimate is
retained, but its score calls for tighter optimization and multiple starting
values. Kernel starting order and the fixed initial state can affect the selected
local solution.

```{r multi-kernel-curvature}
fit_diagnostics(fit_mk)[c("status", "newton_decrement", "warnings")]
```

Reconstruction retains `type_col_map` and the supplied initial intensity matrix.
Each kernel uses its own decay rate in the likelihood and residual integrals.
The inferred likelihood agrees with the fitted likelihood even though decay
rates differ within each row.

```{r multi-kernel-reconstruction, message=FALSE}
estimated_mk <- fitted_hspec(fit_mk)
initial_mk <- fit_initial_state(fit_mk)
estimated_mk@type_col_map
initial_mk$lambda_component0
inferred_mk <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated_mk,
  inter_arrival = res_mk$inter_arrival, type = res_mk$type, infer = TRUE), initial_mk))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(fit_mk)), restored = inferred_mk$loglikelihood)
all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_mk)), inferred_mk$loglikelihood)
```

### Synchronized intensity model

This is a two-kernel model with the following reparameterization.

$$
 \mu = \begin{bmatrix} \theta/(1 - \kappa)/2 + \tilde\theta/(1 + \kappa)/2 \\
\theta/(1 - \kappa)/2 - \tilde\theta/(1 + \kappa)/2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \theta = (\theta^- + \theta^+)/2,\quad \tilde\theta=(\theta^- -\theta^+)/2
$$

$$
\alpha = \begin{bmatrix} \zeta & \tilde\zeta & \zeta & -\tilde\zeta \\
\zeta & -\tilde\zeta & \zeta & \tilde\zeta
\end{bmatrix}, \quad \zeta = (\eta + \nu) / 2, \quad \tilde \zeta = (\eta - \nu)/ 2 
$$

$$
\beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_1 & \beta_2 & \beta_1 & \beta_2 \\
\beta_1 & \beta_2 & \beta_1 & \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \beta_1 = \beta(1 - \kappa), \quad \beta_2 = \beta(1 + \kappa)
$$

To implement this reparameterization, define `mu`, `alpha`, and `beta` as functions.
Each function takes a named parameter vector, `param`, as its first argument.

```{r}
mu <- function(param = c(theta_p = 0.15, theta_n = 0.21, kappa = 0.12)){
  theta    <- (param["theta_n"] + param["theta_p"])/2
  theta_tl <- (param["theta_n"] - param["theta_p"])/2
  matrix(c(theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) + theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"]),
           theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) - theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"])), nrow=2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(eta = 5, nu = 3)){
  zeta    <- (param["eta"] + param["nu"])/2
  zeta_tl <- (param["eta"] - param["nu"])/2
  matrix(c(zeta, zeta_tl, zeta, -zeta_tl,
           zeta, -zeta_tl, zeta, zeta_tl), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
}

beta <- function(param = c(beta = 12, kappa = 0.12)){
  beta1 <- param["beta"] * (1 - param["kappa"])
  beta2 <- param["beta"] * (1 + param["kappa"])
  matrix(c(beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2,
           beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}

type_col_map <- list(c(1,2), c(3,4))

h_sy <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, type_col_map = type_col_map)
h_sy

```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
# run simulation
res_sy <- hsim(h_sy, size = 2000, lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 2 * 4), nrow=2))
summary(res_sy)
```

The parameters to estimate and their initial values are taken from the default `param` vectors.
Parameters with the same name are shared across functions.
For example, `kappa` appears in both `mu` and `beta`, but only one `kappa` is estimated.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit_sy <- hfit(h_sy, inter_arrival=res_sy$inter_arrival,
               type=res_sy$type,
               lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 2 * 4), nrow=2),
               final_hessian = "stable")
summary(fit_sy)
```

The restored component functions use the estimated defaults.
Both functions retain the same estimated `kappa`. Their parameter-only interface
also allows automatic C++ likelihood and residual replay with the saved initial state.

```{r shared-function-parameters}
estimated_sy <- fitted_hspec(fit_sy)
c(mu = eval(formals(estimated_sy@mu)$param)[["kappa"]],
  beta = eval(formals(estimated_sy@beta)$param)[["kappa"]])
```

```{r shared-function-replay}
replayed_sy <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated_sy,
  inter_arrival = res_sy$inter_arrival, type = res_sy$type, infer = TRUE),
  fit_initial_state(fit_sy)))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(fit_sy)), replayed = replayed_sy$loglikelihood)
```

## Extended models

The package supports the following family of extended multivariate marked Hawkes models:

$$
 \lambda(t) = \mu + \int_{(-\infty,t)\times E} h(t, u, z)M(du \times dz)
$$

where the kernel $h$ is

$$
h(t, u, z) = (\alpha + g(t, z))\Gamma(t),
$$

The components are:

-   $\alpha$ is a constant matrix.

-   $g(t, z)$ describes additional effects on the intensities and may depend on the mark or the history of the underlying processes.

-   $\Gamma(t)$ is a matrix of exponential decay terms, with $\Gamma_{ij}(t) = e^{-\beta_{ij}t}$.

-   $M$ is a vector of random measures on the product of the time and mark spaces.

### Linear impact model

In the linear impact model,

$$
 g(t, z) = \eta (z-1).
$$

The `impact` function represents $g(t, z)$, the additional effect of a mark on future intensity.
For details, see [Marked Hawkes process modeling of price dynamics and volatility estimation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0927539816300810).

Its first argument, `param`, contains the model parameters.
Additional arguments, such as `n` and `mark`, provide information about the model or realized path.
Include `...` to accept other arguments supplied by the package.
The `rmark` function generates marks during simulation.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow=2)
alpha <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.6, 0.6, 0.75), nrow=2, byrow=T)
beta <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow=2)
rmark <- function(param = c(p=0.65), ...){
  rgeom(1, p=param[1]) + 1
}

impact <- function(param = c(eta1=0.2), alpha, n, mark, ...){
  ma <- matrix(rep(mark[n]-1, 4), nrow = 2)
  ma * matrix( rep(param["eta1"], 4), nrow=2)
}

hi <- new("hspec", mu=mu, alpha=alpha, beta=beta,
          rmark = rmark,
          impact=impact)
hi
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(1107)
res_impact <- hsim(hi, size=1000, lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(0.1,4), nrow=2))
summary(res_impact)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit <- hfit(hi, 
            inter_arrival = res_impact$inter_arrival,
            type = res_impact$type,
            mark = res_impact$mark,
            lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(0.1,4), nrow=2))

summary(fit)
```

For linear mark effects, specify the `eta` slot directly.
The resulting intensity process is

$$
 \lambda(t) = \mu + \int_{(-\infty, t)\times E} (\alpha + \eta (z-1)) e^{-\beta(t-u)}  M(du \times dz).
$$

```{r}

rmark <- function(param = c(p=0.65), ...){
  rgeom(1, p=param[1]) + 1
}

h <-  new("hspec", mu=0.15, alpha=0.7, beta=1.6, eta=0.3,
          rmark = rmark)
h
```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
res <- hsim(h, size = 1000)
summary(res)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit <- hfit(h, 
            inter_arrival = res$inter_arrival,
            type = res$type,
            mark = res$mark)
summary(fit)
```

To estimate the parameters of the mark distribution as well, supply its density or probability mass function in the `dmark` slot.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
h_md <- h

h_md@dmark <- function(param = c(p = 0.1), n=n, mark=mark, ...){
   dgeom(mark[n] - 1, prob = param["p"])
}

mle_md <- hfit(h_md, 
               inter_arrival = res$inter_arrival, type = res$type, mark = res$mark)
summary(mle_md)
```

The density and generator use the same parameter name, `p`.
Reconstruction updates `rmark` with the value estimated through `dmark`, so new
simulations use the fitted mark distribution. Generator parameters that do not
match estimated coefficient names keep their original defaults.

```{r fitted-mark-generator}
estimated_md <- fitted_hspec(mle_md)
c(density = eval(formals(estimated_md@dmark)$param)[["p"]],
  generator = eval(formals(estimated_md@rmark)$param)[["p"]])
```

### Fosset's state-dependent spread model {#fosset-spread-model}

Fosset, Bouchaud and Benzaquen (2020),
[Endogenous Liquidity Crises](https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-5468/ab7c64),
Section 4.1, equations (8a)--(8b), model spread widening and narrowing as two
event types. Let $N_+$ and $N_-$ count these events and let the spread, in ticks, be

$$
S(t) = S_0 + N_+(t) - N_-(t).
$$

Their linear model has predictable intensities

$$
\lambda_+(t) = \nu_+ + a\int_{[0,t)} b e^{-b(t-s)}\,dN_+(s),
\qquad
\lambda_-(t) = \nu_-\,\mathbf{1}_{\{S(t-)\ge 2\}}.
$$

Only widening events excite future widening. Narrowing is disabled at a one-tick
spread. We use $\nu_+,\nu_-$ for the paper's $\lambda_0^+,\lambda_0^-$ and
$a,b$ for its $\alpha,\beta$. The package's `alpha[1, 1]` is therefore $ab$;
$a$ is the integrated excitation, not the jump size. The other `alpha` entries
are fixed zeros. Both event types have unit marks.

The example uses positive rates, $0<a<1$, and an explicit zero initial excitation.
This restricts the example to a Hawkes-stable widening process. A stationary
spread additionally requires $\nu_+/(1-a)<\nu_-$. The values below are chosen
for a stationary-spread illustration. The nonlinear models later in the paper
are separate specifications.

The following local example helpers are stored with the installed package.
Log rates enforce positivity, and a logit parameter enforces $0<a<1$.
The shared name `log_b` keeps the same decay parameter in `alpha` and `beta`.

```{r fosset-source, include=FALSE}
fosset_example_code <- readLines(
  system.file("examples", "fosset-spread.R", package = "emhawkes"), warn = FALSE)
```

```{r fosset-specification, code=fosset_example_code}
```

For the baseline callback, `N[n - 1, ]` describes the state before event `n`.
The same callback is called with `n + 1` after the jump, so the narrowing rate
changes immediately when the spread reaches or leaves one tick.

```{r fosset-simulation}
h_fosset <- fosset_spec()
set.seed(20261018)
path_fosset <- hsim(h_fosset, size = 4001, lambda_component0 = 0)
spread_fosset <- 1 + path_fosset$N[, 1] - path_fosset$N[, 2]
stopifnot(all(spread_fosset >= 1),
  all(path_fosset$lambda[c(1, head(spread_fosset, -1)) == 1, 2] == 0),
  all(path_fosset$rambda[spread_fosset == 1, 2] == 0))
plot(path_fosset$arrival, spread_fosset, type = "s",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Spread (ticks)")
```

Estimate all four model parameters from a different starting point. The example
uses R's stats optimizer and the default numerical gradient. Automatic engine
selection uses the supported C++ likelihood; simulation of this count-dependent
baseline uses the R path. No analytic Jacobians are required.

```{r fosset-fit}
start_fosset <- fosset_spec(nu_plus = 0.7, nu_minus = 2.5, a = 0.25, b = 1.2)
fit_fosset <- hfit(start_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  lambda_component0 = 0, optimizer = "stats", method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 500, reltol = 1e-10))
cbind(true = c(nu_plus = 1, nu_minus = 3, a = 0.4, b = 2),
  estimated = fosset_parameters(coef(fit_fosset)))
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$status
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$computation$engine
```

The estimated coefficients are on the log/logit scale. Parameter recovery varies
between realizations; inspect convergence and uncertainty rather than expecting
exact recovery from a single path.

There is an independent check for the narrowing rate. If $T_{\mathrm{open}}$ is the
time spent with $S\ge2$, its log-likelihood contribution is
$N_-(T)\log\nu_- - \nu_- T_{\mathrm{open}}$. Its maximum is
$\widehat{\nu}_- = N_-(T)/T_{\mathrm{open}}$.
The observation window ends at the last supplied event.

```{r fosset-check}
open_time_fosset <- sum(path_fosset$inter_arrival[-1] *
  (head(spread_fosset, -1) >= 2))
c(fitted = fosset_parameters(coef(fit_fosset))["nu_minus"],
  independent = sum(path_fosset$type == 2) / open_time_fosset)
restored_fosset <- fitted_hspec(fit_fosset)
replay_fosset <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = restored_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(fit_fosset)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_fosset)),
  unname(replay_fosset$loglikelihood), tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

### Hawkes flocking model

The function $g$ need not depend on the mark.
In the Hawkes flocking model, the kernel components are
$$
\alpha = \begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} & 0 & 0 \\\alpha_{12}& \alpha_{11} & 0 & 0 \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{33} & \alpha_{34} \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{34} & \alpha_{33} \end{bmatrix},
$$ 
$$ 
g = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \alpha_{1w} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} \\ 
0 & 0 & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1w}1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} \\
\alpha_{2w} 1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2n}1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \\
\alpha_{2n} 1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2w}1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
$$

where

$$
C_1(t) = N_1(t) - N_2(t), \quad C_2(t) = N_3(t) - N_4(t).
$$
For details, see [Systemic risk in market microstructure of crude oil and gasoline futures prices: A Hawkes flocking model approach](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/fut.22048).

The `alpha` slot can contain a function that returns a matrix.
In the following example, the function returns a $4\times4$ matrix with some entries fixed at zero.
Only the parameters in `param` are estimated.
For simulation, a fixed matrix and a function returning the same matrix give the same model.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.02, 0.04, 0.04), nrow = 4)


alpha <- function(param = c(alpha11 = 0.2, alpha12 = 0.3, alpha33 = 0.3, alpha34 = 0.4)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha11"], param["alpha12"], 0, 0,
           param["alpha12"], param["alpha11"], 0, 0,
           0, 0, param["alpha33"], param["alpha34"],
           0, 0, param["alpha34"], param["alpha33"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}


beta <- matrix(c(rep(0.7, 8), rep(1.1, 8)), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

```

The `impact` function below implements the model definition.
Its `N` argument contains the counting process values, and `n` identifies the current event index.
Include both arguments because the function uses them, along with `...` to accept other arguments supplied by the package.
Use `N[n, "N1"]` to read one count directly, rather than extracting an entire column at every event.

```{r}
impact <- function(param = c(alpha1n=0.25, alpha1w=0.1, alpha2n=0.1, alpha2w=0.2),
                   N=N, n=n, ...){
  
  Psi <- matrix(c(0, 0, param['alpha1w'], param['alpha1n'],
                  0, 0, param['alpha1n'], param['alpha1w'],
                  param['alpha2w'], param['alpha2n'], 0, 0,
                  param['alpha2n'], param['alpha2w'], 0, 0), nrow=4, byrow=TRUE)
  
  ind <- N[n,"N1"] - N[n,"N2"] > N[n,"N3"] - N[n,"N4"]
  
  km <- matrix(c(!ind, !ind, !ind, !ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 !ind, !ind, !ind, !ind), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
  
  km * Psi
}

hspec_fl <- new("hspec",
                mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact = impact)
hspec_fl
```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
hr_fl <- hsim(hspec_fl, size=2000)
summary(hr_fl)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
fit_fl <- hfit(hspec_fl, hr_fl$inter_arrival, hr_fl$type)
summary(fit_fl)
```

This impact depends on observed event counts, so automatic selection uses the
C++ likelihood with numerical differentiation. No Jacobian is needed; R still
evaluates the impact.

```{r flocking-engine}
fit_diagnostics(fit_fl)$computation$engine
```

The same observed impact also supports automatic C++ intensity and residual replay.
No Jacobian is needed; retain the fit's initial-state arguments.

```{r flocking-replay}
replayed_fl <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = fitted_hspec(fit_fl),
  inter_arrival = hr_fl$inter_arrival, type = hr_fl$type, infer = TRUE),
  fit_initial_state(fit_fl)))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(fit_fl)), replayed = replayed_fl$loglikelihood)
```

### Bid-ask price model

This model describes bid and ask prices using a system of counting processes and their conditional intensities:

$$ 
N_t = \begin{bmatrix}
N_1(t) \\ N_2(t) \\ N_3(t) \\ N_4(t)
\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\lambda_t =
\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(t) \\ \lambda_2(t) \\ \lambda_3(t) \\ \lambda_4(t)
\end{bmatrix}
$$

In the unmarked case, the changes in ask and bid prices are $N_1(t) - N_2(t)$ and $N_3(t) - N_4(t)$, respectively.
The marked example below uses `Nc` to accumulate price changes.
The midprice $p(t)$ is the average of the ask and bid prices, including their initial levels.

The base intensity process is

$$\mu = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \mu_1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \ell(t) = \frac{L(t)}{p(t)} $$

where $L(t) \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ measures the bid-ask spread above its minimum level, so $L(t)=0$ corresponds to the minimum spread.
For details, see [Modeling bid and ask price dynamics with an extended Hawkes process and its empirical applications for high-frequency stock market data](https://academic.oup.com/jfec/article/21/4/1099/6513935?login=true).

In the `mu` function below, `n` identifies the current event index, and `Nc` is used to calculate the spread level and midprice.

```{r}
# presumed initial bid and ask prices
initial_ask_price <- 1250 #cents
initial_bid_price <- 1150 #cents

initial_level <- round((initial_ask_price - initial_bid_price) - 1)
initial_mid_price <- (initial_bid_price + initial_ask_price) / 2

mu <- function(param = c(mu1 = 0.08, zeta1 = 0.10), n=n, Nc=Nc, ...){

  if(n == 1){
    
    level <- initial_level
    mid <- initial_mid_price
    
  } else {
    
    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2]) 
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) 
    mid <- (ask + bid) / 2
    
  }
  
  if(level <= 0){
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], 0,
             0, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)
  } else {
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], param["zeta1"] * level / mid,
             param["zeta1"]*level / mid, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)

  }

}
```

In addition, the kernel is represented by

$$h(t, u) = 
\begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{s1} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s2} & 0 \\   \alpha_{w1} & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{w2} \\  \alpha_{w2} & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{w1} \\  0 & \alpha_{s2} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s1} \\   \end{bmatrix},
$$

where

$$
\alpha_{n1}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{2j}(u) + \xi \ell(u), \quad \alpha_{n2}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{3j}(u) + \xi \ell(u),
$$

Here, $\xi \geq 0$ is a constant, and $\lambda_{ij}$ is a component of $\lambda_i$, defined by

$$\lambda_{ij}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^t h_{ij}(t, u) d N_j(u).$$

The following code places the constant part of $h$ in `alpha` and the state-dependent part in `impact`.
The `lambda_component_n` argument supplies the current pre-jump matrix of $\lambda_{ij}$ values.
This avoids allocating a full intensity history when only the current state is needed.
Individual components can be negative after a reset.
The equal decay rates used here allow simulation as long as the sum of the components in each row remains nonnegative.

```{r, warning=FALSE}

alpha <- function(param = c(alpha_s1=4, alpha_m=26, alpha_s2=5,
                            alpha_w1=11, alpha_w2=7)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha_s1"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s2"], 0,
           param["alpha_w1"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w2"],
           param["alpha_w2"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w1"],
           0, param["alpha_s2"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s1"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}

impact <- function(param = c(xi = 2.7), n=n, Nc=Nc, lambda_component_n = lambda_component_n, ... ){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
    # mid <- initial_mid_price
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2] - (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2])
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4])
    mid <- (ask + bid)/2
  }
  
  lambda_component_matrix <- lambda_component_n

  l2 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[2,]) # sum of second row
  l3 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[3,]) # sum of third row

  im <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0, 0,
                 0, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

}

beta <- matrix(rep(50, 16), nrow = 4, byrow=TRUE)

rmark <- function(n=n, Nc=Nc, type, ...){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
  }
  if (type[n] == 2 | type[n] == 3){
    min(level,  rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1)
  } else {
    rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1
  }
}


h_ba <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact=impact, rmark = rmark)
h_ba
```

```{r}
set.seed(1107)
hr_ba <- hsim(h_ba, size=1000, lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4))
summary(hr_ba)
```

The following likelihood calculation and fit do not estimate the mark distribution because no `dmark` function is supplied.

```{r}
logLik(h_ba, inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type,
       mark = hr_ba$mark, Nc = hr_ba$Nc,
       lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4))
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mle_ba <- hfit(h_ba, inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type,
               mark = hr_ba$mark,
               lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4),
               final_hessian = "stable")
summary(mle_ba)
```

Automatic selection uses the C++ likelihood for this observed baseline and
sequential impact with numerical differentiation. The impact reads the current
state before its jump. No Jacobian is required. Inspect the saved engine record
to confirm which calculation was used and whether automatic selection fell back to R.

This example needs only the current component matrix, so it uses
`lambda_component_n`. Requesting `lambda_component` also stores the full history.
If a callback retains histories beyond its call, preserving those snapshots can
copy the history repeatedly. Cumulative allocation can then grow quadratically
with event count. This cost is
repeated for each likelihood evaluation during numerical optimization. Peak live
memory can be much smaller because old copies are reclaimed.

```{r bid-ask-engine}
fit_diagnostics(mle_ba)$computation$engine
```

Replay the fitted model with the same initialization and observations. Automatic
selection also uses C++ for its likelihood, intensity paths, and residuals.

```{r bid-ask-replay}
replayed_ba <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = fitted_hspec(mle_ba),
  inter_arrival = hr_ba$inter_arrival, type = hr_ba$type, mark = hr_ba$mark,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(mle_ba)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(replayed_ba$loglikelihood),
  as.numeric(mle_ba$maximum), tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

For the optional analytic fit, see the
[Bid-ask Jacobians and analytic gradient](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/computation.html#bid-ask-analytic-gradient).
That section continues from this example and gives the complete derivatives and fit.
Numerical differentiation remains the default.

## Point processes with flexible residuals

FRPP-specific functionality is planned to move to the separate
[frpp package](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/). Use its
[FRPP examples](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/articles/frpp-examples.html)
for `fspec()`, `fsim()` and `ffit()`. The full examples previously shown here,
including the original emhawkes fitting code, are preserved in the
[compatibility vignette](https://ksublee.github.io/frpp/articles/emhawkes-compatibility.html).

Simple custom-residual models can still use `set_residual()`, `hsim()` and
`logLik()` in emhawkes. These functions remain available during the transition;
this documentation change does not remove or deprecate them. For example:

```{r simple-flexible-residual, message=FALSE}
h_residual <- set_residual(
  new("hspec", mu = 0.5, alpha = 1, beta = 1.2),
  param = c(a = 0.7, ell = 1.6),
  dresidual = dtzexp, presidual = ptzexp,
  qresidual = qtzexp, rresidual = rtzexp
)
set.seed(1107)
path_residual <- hsim(h_residual, size = 100, lambda_component0 = 0)
logLik(h_residual, inter_arrival = path_residual$inter_arrival,
       lambda_component0 = 0)
```

Hawkes goodness-of-fit residual diagnostics remain part of emhawkes; see
[Fitting and inference](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/fitting-and-inference.html#residual-process).
